stops.name: Francavilla al Mare, the Conventino of Michetti, Il Piacere written
stops.campa: In the summer of 1888 he shuts himself in the sea-facing convent that Francesco Paolo Michetti has made his studio at Francavilla. The cenacolo gathers: Michetti painting, Tosti at the piano, Barbella modelling clay, the poet writing in monastic fury. In six months of Adriatic light he composes Il Piacere, giving Rome its Andrea Sperelli: the aesthete as hero, the life made artwork. Treves publishes it in May 1889 and the novel fixes the type of the Italian decadent forever. The convent, he says, is his true university.

stops.name: San Vito Chietino, the Eremo on the Trabocchi coast, with Barbara Leoni
stops.campa: Summer 1889: with Barbara Leoni, the great erotic passion of the Roman years, he takes a hermitage above the trabocchi: the spider-legged fishing machines of the Chieti coast. The ginestra blazes on the cliff; the lovers live on bread, fruit and each other. Out of this summer he will build Il Trionfo della Morte, setting Giorgio Aurispa's final leap from these very rocks. The landscape is promoted to scripture: the Abruzzo coast enters European literature as a place where love and death share one house.

stops.name: Rome, the cavalry year with the Cavalleggeri di Alessandria
stops.campa: Called at last to military service, the aesthete astonishes everyone by excelling at it. A year with the Cavalleggeri di Alessandria: he rides superbly, endures gladly, and discovers in the barracks a taste that will outlast every drawing-room: the taste for soldiering. The officers find the famous poet the hardest man in the squadron to tire. Horse, saber, trumpet at dawn: the future Comandante is founded here, though for now he returns his commission and goes back to his debts and his novels.

stops.name: Naples, arrival into the splendid misery
stops.campa: Fleeing Roman creditors in August 1891, he comes down to Naples for a fortnight and stays two years. He will call it his splendida miseria: pawned watches, borrowed dress-shirts, and meanwhile the richest prose of his life. Naples gives him Wagner in the salons, the Neapolitan press at his feet, and the Countess Maria Gravina di Ramacca, who abandons husband and children for him and is convicted of adultery beside him. He is poor as a saint and lives like a cardinal.

stops.name: Corriere di Napoli, L'Innocente in serial, the name crosses the Alps
stops.campa: In the pages of Scarfoglio and Serao's Corriere di Napoli, L'Innocente runs in serial through the winter: the Tolstoyan novel of a husband who lets his wife's bastard die of the cold. France reads it as L'Intrus and Europe learns the name d'Annunzio; Eleonora Duse reads it and writes to the author she has not yet met, asking him for a work worthy of her. The letter is an annunciation he files away. Giovanni Episcopo follows; the Russian masters have passed through him and come out Latin.

stops.name: Francavilla al Mare, Il Trionfo della Morte finished at the Conventino
stops.campa: Back under Michetti's roof, ruined and radiant, he completes Il Trionfo della Morte, the book of the Trabocchi coast and of Barbara, Ippolita in its pages, and dedicates it to Michetti himself. The novel closes the Romances of the Rose: desire studied until it becomes fatal. From Naples he has carried Nietzsche north in his baggage; the Superman enters Italian letters through an Abruzzo convent window. The province that made him now has its epic of blood, saints' shrines and the deaf pull of the sea.

stops.name: Athens, the cruise of the Fantasia, Greece touched with the hands
stops.campa: In the summer of 1895 he sails the Aegean on Scarfoglio's yacht Fantasia with Georges Hérelle, his French translator, aboard. Patras, Olympia, Mycenae, Athens: he climbs the Acropolis in white flannel and takes possession of Hellas as a legacy owed to him. The companions record seasickness and brothels; he records the marble and the light. From this cruise the Laus Vitae of Maia will rise years later: eight thousand verses making the voyage into the myth of Ulysses renewed in an Italian body.
stops.quote: O Vita, o Vita, dono terribile del dio, come una spada fedele, come una ruggente face...

stops.name: Venice, the Hotel Danieli, Eleonora Duse
stops.campa: On 26 September 1895, at the Hotel Danieli, the poet and Eleonora Duse are joined at last. She has read the Trionfo and calls him the infernal poet; after the first night she sends him a note of three words, Vedo il sole, I see the sun, and names the meeting a solar enchantment. The greatest actress alive and the poet who intends to be the greatest anything alive: for eight years Italian theatre will be their correspondence made flesh. The lagoon seals the pact.

stops.name: Venice, L'Allegoria dell'Autunno in the Doge's Palace
stops.campa: In November 1895, for the city that has just invented its Biennale, he delivers L'Allegoria dell'Autunno: Venice preached to Venice, the dying season made a theory of art. The orator discovers his second instrument: not the page but the vaulted hall, the crowd breathing with the sentence. Out of this autumn will come Il Fuoco and its Stelio Effrena, the imaginary orator whose speeches the real one has already given. Venice is annexed to the legend; the legend will repay her with the Casetta Rossa and the Notturno.

stops.name: Pescara, the Discorso della siepe, the deputy of Beauty
stops.campa: In August 1897 he stands for parliament in the college of Ortona as the candidato della Bellezza, the candidate of Beauty, and at a banquet near Pescara delivers the Discorso della siepe, the Speech of the Hedge: property, land and the peasant's hedge sung as sacred forms. The Abruzzo, amused and proud, elects its poet. He enters Montecitorio announcing that he brings culture among the barbarians, and votes rarely, gloriously, and only for spectacle. Politics has been annexed to aesthetics; the rehearsal for Fiume begins here.

stops.name: Settignano, La Capponcina taken, the court of the borzois
stops.campa: Above Florence, at Settignano, he installs himself in the villa La Capponcina and furnishes it like a Renaissance reliquary on credit: damasks, lecterns, casts of the Parthenon frieze, forty greyhounds and borzois, horses named out of Ariosto. Eleonora Duse takes the Porziuncola close by; the two houses signal to each other across the olive terraces. Here he writes standing at a monk's desk, dressed like a Quattrocento page. The creditors circle for twelve years before they are permitted to exist.

stops.name: La Capponcina, La Gioconda for the Duse of the beautiful hands
stops.campa: For Eleonora he writes La Gioconda, the tragedy of the sculptor between wife and muse, and sets on its threshold the most courtly dedication in the Italian theatre: to Eleonora Duse of the beautiful hands. In the play the wife's hands are crushed saving the rival's statue; Duse plays the mutilation nightly with her sleeves pinned empty. The public understands that the poet gives his lover masterpieces the way other men give rings, and that every gift is also a wound prepared in advance.
stops.quote: A Eleonora Duse dalle belle mani.
